correctness.rationale: For every \(r\ge2\) and shore sizes at least two, tensor adjacency pairs each shore pattern only with its complement, producing \(2^{r-1}\) biclique components. Exactly one chosen vertex per component shore is necessary and sufficient for total-perfect-code status. This forces the exact count, Hamming-product exchange graph, and distance formula. The product-code distance distribution counts per-factor agreements; the covering-radius bound selects complementary patterns, and injective coordinates prove sharpness under the declared size condition. The embedded C++ verifier checks all \(2^{16}\) and \(2^{20}\) subsets in two cases; a separately coded Python verifier checks finite configurations and a three-factor sharpness witness. Every infinite statement has a finite-free combinatorial proof in RESULT.md.

originality.rationale: The closest fully inspected primary paper (Abay-Asmerom, Hammack and Taylor 2008, publisher PDF pp. 129-134) proves the tensor-product existence theorem and shows by examples that factor counts alone do not determine product counts. It does not state or imply as a numerical general theorem the full tensor-biclique code count, complete exchange product, product-code exact distance distribution, or sharp covering radius. A 2006 component theorem is strictly about graph decomposition. Searches for efficient-open-domination and total-perfect-code aliases identified related but distinct four-cube and Gray-graph results, and no covering exact claim. Residual priority risk of unindexed equivalent work remains.
residual_risks: An unindexed thesis or prior paper might contain an equivalent tensor-biclique counting or reconfiguration formula.
The 2006 component paper and some relevant later mathematical records were checked at abstract/claim level rather than full text; no covering code assertion was exposed.
Reproducibility programs verify only finite cases; the general proof is combinatorial and independent scholarly audit has not been performed.

value.rationale: The biclique family is the simplest freely parameterized family in which tensor products split into many nontrivial components; the 2008 foundational result specifically raises the gap between product codes and all codes by proving existence and giving examples where counts do not factor. The new exact full count and Hamming exchange classification quantify that gap, while an exact factorwise distance spectrum and sharp covering radius show sparse factorable optima are both sharply separated and surprisingly close to every non-factorable optimum. This is an all-parameter structural classification with sharp geometry, not a minor numerical update or an arbitrary finite slice.
